precepts.text: Esau, seeing that the daughters of Canaan pleased not Isaac his father, went unto Ishmael, and took Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael Abraham's son to be his wife. So now he married Arab kids too; that is what Esau was doing.
precepts.point: Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. In that pottage was meat: feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage, raw, bloody meat. And you have brothers today lusting after these same people. Many times brothers ask what it means that Esau was profane or a fornicator; the scriptures explain it.

note.label: We Are Born in Babylon

precepts.why:
After the Hittite wives, Esau went further: “Esau seeing that the daughters of Canaan pleased not Isaac his father; Then went Esau unto Ishmael, and took unto the wives which he had Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael Abraham’s son, the sister of Nebajoth, to be his wife.”

Esau saw that Isaac was pissed off that he married the daughters of Canaan, and instead of turning back to his own kindred, he went to Ishmael. So now he married Arab kids too. That is what Esau was doing: taking wives outside his father's tribe, one after another.

That is the fornication Hebrews 12:16 names. Esau married the Hittites and the Ishmaelites, strange women, and he was profane because for “one morsel of meat” he sold his birthright; it meant a lot, and he did not care about it.

precepts.text: Jacob's name changed to Israel: a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee. Prophetically the nation is the southern kingdom and the company of nations the northern kingdom.
precepts.point: In thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed: the Israelite families in those lands, not the nations, whose blessing is servitude.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.why:
At Bethel the Lord promised Jacob, “thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth, and thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south”. Israel would be everywhere on the earth, through captivity and through migration, forced or willing. And the promise goes on, “and in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed”: that is the Israelite families in those lands, north, south, east and west. The nations are not the ones blessed; their blessing is servitude.

Then the Lord renamed him: “Thy name is Jacob: thy name shall not be called any more Jacob, but Israel shall be thy name”. “I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee, and kings shall come out of thy loins”. In context that can mean all twelve tribes, but prophetically it is written that way for the division to come: the nation is the southern kingdom, Judah, and the company of nations is the northern kingdom, Ephraim. The kings out of his loins are Saul, David, Hezekiah and Josiah.

Moses shows where the division came from. “When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel. For the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.” He kept us “as the apple of his eye.” “But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked”, rich, comfortable and rebellious, and “lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation”, which is Christ. So the Lord said, “I will move them to jealousy with those which are not a people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.” Isaiah names who is not a people: “within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people”, after the northern kingdom joined Syria against Judah.

Hosea says the same of the company of nations: “Call his name Lo–ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.” Ephraim became as Gentiles, heathens, the uncircumcision. “But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah”. Yet the number of Israel “shall be as the sand of the sea”, as promised to Jacob, and “in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God. Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint themselves one head”, and that head is Christ. Ezekiel agrees: “they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all”.

The hatred between the nation and the company of nations is why both fell, the north first and Judah after. The law always said, “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart”, and “he that hateth his brother is in darkness”. Esau never forgets and holds his grudges, while Jacob in captivity forgets his own and cares more for his oppressor. The people that enslaved us tortured us, beat us, raped us, castrated us and hid our history for hundreds of years, and now they are ruling: that is their heaven, and we are in hell. Imagine being in the heathen's hell and teaching the devil in his kingdom the access he has to heaven, our heaven. That's hate. You hate your people and you hate yourself, and for that you are in darkness. In captivity, your people being oppressed, and all you care about is your oppressor: you're a dummy, and that is the kindest word for it. Love your people and love your ways, and the nation and the company of nations become one again.

precepts.text: Esau took Ishmael's daughter to spite his father, and Jacob's seed was promised to spread to the four corners.
precepts.point: Joseph saved Israel in the famine and Joshua of Ephraim divided the land. Ephraim therefore felt more entitled than Judah, and the rivalry began long before the split.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.why:
“When Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob, and sent him away to Padan–aram, to take him a wife from thence; and that as he blessed him he gave him a charge, saying, Thou shalt not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan; And that Jacob obeyed his father and his mother”, Esau, seeing “that the daughters of Canaan pleased not Isaac his father”, went his own rebellious way anyway. “Then went Esau unto Ishmael, and took unto the wives which he had Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael Abraham’s son”. That is how Ishmael and Esau started intermingling, and that is where the light-skinned Arabs come from.

Jacob went toward Haran, and at a certain place he dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven, “and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.” The Lord promised, “the land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed; And thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth, and thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south”. That is all four corners: before they were even born, it was prophesied that Jacob’s seed would be found in the four corners of the earth, scattered among the families of the earth, “and in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed.” And the Lord promised, “I will not leave thee, until I have done that which I have spoken to thee of.”

Jacob said, “this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven”, a portal to paradise. He set up his stone for a pillar, poured oil on it, “And he called the name of that place Beth–el: but the name of that city was called Luz at the first.” He vowed the tenth, the tithe.

Keep Bethel in mind. On the map it sits right under Shechem, the place where Abraham first built an altar in Canaan and where Rehoboam was later crowned. These early holy places all lay in the land that would become Ephraim’s.

precepts.text: The fathers from the beginning married wives of their own kindred; take a wife of the seed of thy fathers.
precepts.point: With the charge came the blessing of Abraham, passed now to Jacob and his seed: to be fruitful, to multiply into a multitude of people, and to inherit the land promised to Abraham.

note.label: Genesis 28: The Charge and the Vow at Bethel

precepts.why:
Isaac charged Jacob, “Thou shalt not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan”, but to go to the house of Bethuel and take a wife of the daughters of Laban. Tobit shows this was the way of the fathers from the beginning: “take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife, which is not of thy father’s tribe: for we are the children of the prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: remember, my son, that our fathers from the beginning, even that they all married wives of their own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall inherit the land.”

Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob married wives of their own kindred and were blessed in their children. And with the charge came the blessing: to be fruitful, to multiply into “a multitude of people”, and to “inherit the land wherein thou art a stranger, which God gave unto Abraham.” Their seed shall inherit the land.

precepts.text: Abraham made his servant swear the same charge for Isaac: no wife of the daughters of the Canaanites, but of his own kindred.
precepts.point: With the charge came the blessing of Abraham, passed now to Jacob and his seed: to be fruitful, to multiply into a multitude of people, and to inherit the land promised to Abraham.

note.label: Genesis 28: The Charge and the Vow at Bethel

precepts.why:
Isaac gives Jacob the charge his own father gave for him. Abraham made his eldest servant swear “that thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell: But thou shalt go unto my country, and to my kindred, and take a wife unto my son Isaac.”

Now Isaac says the same to Jacob: not of the daughters of Canaan, but of the daughters of Laban thy mother’s brother. The instruction was kept in the family line from the beginning, and with it passed the blessing of Abraham, to Jacob and to his seed with him.

precepts.text: Rebekah was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother; the marriages stayed within the kindred.
precepts.point: Jacob was sent to Laban, the son of Bethuel the Syrian, the brother of Rebekah. Rebekah herself was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother; the family line was kept in place, generation after generation going back to their own kindred.

note.label: Genesis 28: The Charge and the Vow at Bethel

precepts.why:
Jacob was sent “unto Laban, son of Bethuel the Syrian, the brother of Rebekah.” Rebekah herself came out of that same house: she “was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother.”

Nahor was Abraham’s brother; Bethuel was Nahor’s son; Rebekah was Bethuel’s daughter; and now Jacob goes to Bethuel’s son Laban for a wife. The family line was kept in place, generation after generation going back to their own kindred.

precepts.text: Esau's Hittite wives were a grief of mind unto Isaac and Rebekah.
precepts.point: Esau had already taken Hittite wives that were a grief of mind unto Isaac and Rebekah, and his generations show wives of the daughters of Canaan. He was hardheaded from the beginning; that is the spirit of the wicked, who hate instruction and cast the words of the Most High behind them.

note.label: Genesis 28: The Charge and the Vow at Bethel

precepts.why:
Esau had already taken wives that grieved his parents. “Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite: Which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah.”

So when Esau saw “that the daughters of Canaan pleased not Isaac his father”, that was nothing new. He was hardheaded from the beginning. And instead of following Jacob’s path he went to Ishmael and took Mahalath “unto the wives which he had”: he answered his father’s grief by doing his own thing.

precepts.text: Esau's generations confirm he took wives of the daughters of Canaan and of Ishmael.
precepts.point: Esau had already taken Hittite wives that were a grief of mind unto Isaac and Rebekah, and his generations show wives of the daughters of Canaan. He was hardheaded from the beginning; that is the spirit of the wicked, who hate instruction and cast the words of the Most High behind them.

note.label: Genesis 28: The Charge and the Vow at Bethel

precepts.why:
Esau’s generations confirm it. “Esau took his wives of the daughters of Canaan; Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Aholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite; And Bashemath Ishmael’s daughter, sister of Nebajoth.”

Wives of the daughters of Canaan, the Hittite and the Hivite, and then Ishmael’s daughter added on top. He never put away the Canaanite wives that pleased not his father; he took Ishmael’s daughter unto the wives which he had. That is Esau doing his own thing.

precepts.text: Unto the wicked God saith, Thou hatest instruction, and castest my words behind thee; that is Esau's spirit.
precepts.point: Esau had already taken Hittite wives that were a grief of mind unto Isaac and Rebekah, and his generations show wives of the daughters of Canaan. He was hardheaded from the beginning; that is the spirit of the wicked, who hate instruction and cast the words of the Most High behind them.

note.label: Genesis 28: The Charge and the Vow at Bethel

precepts.why:
Esau saw that the daughters of Canaan pleased not his father, and went and did his own thing. That is the spirit of the wicked. “But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth? Seeing thou hatest instruction, and castest my words behind thee.”

Jacob obeyed his father and his mother and went to Padanaram. Esau heard the same charge and cast it behind him. Hating instruction and casting the words of the Most High behind you is Esau’s spirit, and he was hardheaded from the beginning.

precepts.text: When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
precepts.point: A vow to the Most High is not to be made lightly. When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Jacob vowed and rolled with the Most High, and he paid his vow.

note.label: Genesis 28: The Charge and the Vow at Bethel

precepts.why:
Jacob “vowed a vow”: if God will be with him, keep him in the way, give him bread to eat and raiment to put on, and bring him again to his father’s house in peace, “then shall the Lord be my God”, the stone shall be God’s house, and “of all that thou shalt give me I will surely give the tenth unto thee.”

A vow to the Most High is not to be made lightly. “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.” Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not say before the angel that it was an error, “wherefore should God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the work of thine hands?”

Jacob vowed and rolled with the Most High, and he paid his vow.

precepts.text: Isaac charged Jacob to arise and go to Padanaram to the house of Bethuel; that is where Jacob was headed.
precepts.point: This is the same ground the family had already covered. Isaac charged Jacob to go to Padanaram to the house of Bethuel, and generations earlier Terah had brought Abram from Ur of the Chaldees up along the Euphrates, and they came unto Haran and dwelt there.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
Jacob “came into the land of the people of the east” because that is where he was sent. Isaac charged him: “Arise, go to Padan–aram, to the house of Bethuel thy mother’s father; and take thee a wife from thence of the daughters of Laban thy mother’s brother.”

On the map he goes north out of Canaan and then east to Haran in Padanaram. That is why the men at the well answer him, “Of Haran are we.” He had arrived where his father told him to go.

precepts.text: Jacob set up the stone for a pillar and called that place Bethel, but the name of that city was called Luz at the first.
precepts.point: We are reading about it in Joshua where our forefather had already been to that location, and we are just going back to take it back. That is what we are doing.

note.label: Joshua 16: The Lot of the Children of Joseph

precepts.why:
The lot of the children of Joseph goes up through mount Bethel and “goeth out from Beth–el to Luz”. This is the same place where our forefather Jacob was, where he had the vision of the ladder that reached up into heaven. “And Jacob rose up early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put for his pillows, and set it up for a pillar, and poured oil upon the top of it. And he called the name of that place Beth–el: but the name of that city was called Luz at the first.”

So the Bethel and Luz in Joseph's lot are Jacob's Bethel and Luz. We are reading about it in Joshua where our forefather had already been to that location, and we are just going back to take it back. That is what we are doing.

precepts.text: Isaac called Jacob, blessed him, and charged him: thou shalt not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan; the fathers commanded their sons to choose from their own people.
precepts.point: Samson insisted, get her for me, for she pleaseth me well. The forefathers always charged their sons not to do this.

note.label: Judges 14: An Occasion Against the Philistines

precepts.why:
Samson’s parents asked, “Is there never a woman among the daughters of thy brethren, or among all my people, that thou goest to take a wife of the uncircumcised Philistines?” They answered him rightly. The forefathers always charged their sons not to do this: “Isaac called Jacob, and blessed him, and charged him, and said unto him, Thou shalt not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan.”

The fathers commanded their sons to choose from their own people, and there were twelve tribes; there was no shortage of women in all the coasts of Israel. But as he grew up Samson had a lust issue with heathen women, the infamy the story of Samson is known for, and he insisted, “Get her for me; for she pleaseth me well.”

precepts.text: "Thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth... and in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed," part of the promise to Abraham through Israel.
precepts.point: "Ye are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying unto Abraham, And in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed." The "ye" are the children of Israel, and "kindreds" means a lineage or family that descends from a common progenitor, Abraham, not all nations.

note.label: Acts 3: The Restitution of All Things

precepts.why:
The promise to Abraham passed to Jacob: “And thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth, and thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south: and in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed.”

Jacob's seed would spread abroad in every direction, and in that seed all the families of the earth are blessed. The promise runs through Israel, the family of Abraham spread abroad, which is who Peter calls the children of the covenant.
